Numbers from 0 to 1000

In English, 13 to 19 all end in \"-teen\". Italian works differently: 11 to 16 form one family (ending in -dici), then 17, 18 and 19 start with \"ten\" (dici-): diciassette, diciotto, diciannove.

NumberItalianNumberItalian
0zero11undici
1uno12dodici
2due13tredici
3tre14quattordici
4quattro15quindici
5cinque16sedici
6sei17diciassette
7sette18diciotto
8otto19diciannove
9nove20venti
10dieci

The tens

30 trenta · 40 quaranta · 50 cinquanta · 60 sessanta · 70 settanta · 80 ottanta · 90 novanta

Watch out for the look-alikes: sei (6) and sette (7), sessanta (60) and settanta (70). Say them out loud until they sound clearly different to you.

Building numbers: one word, never \"e\"

You stick the ten and the unit together, with no hyphen: venti + due = ventidue. Never say \"venti e uno\": 21 is ventuno. Two rules:

  • Before uno and otto, the ten loses its final vowel: ventuno, ventotto, trentotto, ottantuno.
  • Tre at the end of a number takes an accent: ventitré, trentatré.

Cento and mille

Unlike English \"one hundred\" and \"one thousand\", you don't put \"one\" in front: cento (100), mille (1000). Hundreds are written as one block: duecento, trecento, centoventi (120), trecentocinquanta (350). Cento doesn't change, but mille becomes mila in the plural: duemila, tremila.

La bicicletta costa trecentocinquanta euro.The bike costs three hundred fifty euros.
", "

Days, months and dates

ItalianEnglish
lunedìMonday
martedìTuesday
mercoledìWednesday
giovedìThursday
venerdìFriday
sabatoSaturday
domenicaSunday

Unlike English, the days are written with a lowercase letter. They are masculine, except one: la domenica. The days ending in -dì have an accent on the last syllable.

Lunedì or il lunedì?

ItalianMeaning
Lunedì lavoro a casa.That Monday, just once.
Il lunedì lavoro a casa.On Mondays, every Monday.
La domenica pranzo con i nonni.On Sundays, every Sunday.

English makes the same distinction with \"on Monday\" / \"on Mondays\". The only trap: with domenica, the article is feminine.

Months and dates

gennaio, febbraio, marzo, aprile, maggio, giugno, luglio, agosto, settembre, ottobre, novembre, dicembre: lowercase too, unlike English.

A date is built with il + number + month, day first: il tre giugno (June 3), il venti luglio (July 20). No \"of\" and no \"-th\". Two special cases:

  • The 1st uses the ordinal, like \"the first\": il primo maggio.
  • Before a vowel, il becomes l': l'otto marzo, l'undici settembre.
Che giorno è oggi? Oggi è il diciassette ottobre duemilaventisei.What's the date today? Today is October 17, 2026.
", "

Age and prices

Age: with avere, not \"to be\"

Quanti anni hai? Ho trentadue anni.How old are you? I'm thirty-two. (Literally: how many years do you have? I have thirty-two years.)

Quanti agrees with anni (masculine plural). For someone else: Quanti anni ha Marco?

Prices: the verb agrees with what costs

One thingSeveral things
Quanto costa il libro?Quanto costano le scarpe?
Costa dodici euro.Costano novantotto euro.

Euro doesn't change in the plural: un euro, dieci euro (never \"euros\"). For cents, you simply say tre euro e cinquanta (€3.50).

For the total: Quant'è? (How much is it?) As soon as it's more than one euro, the answer is plural: Sono quaranta euro.

The trap: saying \"quanto costa le scarpe\". Look at the noun: singular, costa; plural, costano.

title: Numbers, days and dates
topic: numbers from 0 to 1000; days, months, dates; age and prices
why: With telling time (My day), the learner already handles numbers up to 24. This lesson extends them to 1000 for what's useful right away when traveling and in daily life: saying your age, understanding a price, giving a date or an opening day, always in the present and with the regular verbs already covered.
